prompt.context: Your client, the general manager of Beta Peaks, a ski mountain in western Massachusetts, has asked you to help him with the business. He was appointed to oversee all business operations 4 years ago. The client has noted that each year, Beta Peaks has earned disproportionately lower revenues than a nearby mountain, Alpha Peaks. While costs have been stable, he is afraid that the mountain cannot stay in business if the current trend continues.
prompt.question: Your assignment is to identify why revenues are lower at Beta Peaks and to propose solutions to increase revenues. What areas would you explore to identify why revenues have declined?

clarifying_info.q: Has total customer demand in the market changed?
clarifying_info.a: Total number of customers has remained constant over the past 4 years.
Alpha Peaks is the only other mountain within 100 miles of Beta Peaks.

clarifying_info.q: Are ticket prices and product mix different between the two mountains?
clarifying_info.a: Prices and product sales mix for all other concessions, rentals, and apparel sales are the same. Alpha Peaks charges $30 for day passes while Beta Peaks charges $40.

exhibits.title: Representative Snapshot of the two mountains
exhibits.shows: A side-by-side comparison table of operational statistics for Beta Peaks and Alpha Peaks

framework: Demand: Has total market demand changed? (No — constant over 4 years)
Competition: Who are the competitors and how do they differ? (Only Alpha Peaks, within 100 miles)
Pricing: Are ticket prices different? (Yes — Beta $40 vs Alpha $30)
Volume/Capacity: How many customers does each mountain handle? (Use lift data to estimate)
Product Mix: Are revenues from concessions, rentals, apparel different? (No — same mix and prices)
Identify root cause and propose solutions to increase Beta Peaks revenue

questions.prompt: Given the data in Exhibit 1, what is the average number of customers at each mountain?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a queuing model (single queue, multiple server). Only chairs going UP count for lift capacity (10 of 20 chairs). Compute people on lifts + people skiing down + people in line for each mountain. Strong candidates recognize Alpha has 3x the customers of Beta, and connect this to the revenue gap.

math.setup: Assume single queue, multiple server model. All lifts have 20 chairs total: 10 going up, 10 going down. Only the 10 chairs going up are used to calculate customers on the lift.
steps: Beta Peaks — People on lifts: 10 chairs/quad x 2 quads x 4 seats/chair = 80 people
Beta Peaks — People skiing down: 8 people arrive at the top per minute x 10 minutes to get down = 80 people
Beta Peaks — People in line: arrival rate x wait time = 8 people/min x 5 min = 40 people
Beta Peaks TOTAL: 80 + 80 + 40 = 200 people
Alpha Peaks — People on lifts: (10 chairs/quad x 2 quads x 4 seats/chair) + (10 chairs/double x 2 doubles x 2 seats/chair) = 80 + 40 = 120 people
Alpha Peaks — People skiing down: 12 people arrive at top per minute x 10 minutes = 120 people
Alpha Peaks — People in line: 12 people/min x 30 min = 360 people
Alpha Peaks TOTAL: 120 + 120 + 360 = 600 people
Revenue comparison: Beta = 200 x $40 = $8,000/day; Alpha = 600 x $30 = $18,000/day; difference = $10,000/day
Beta has 3x fewer customers despite a 6x shorter wait time — significant untapped capacity signal
math.answer: Beta Peaks: 200 customers/day generating $8,000/day. Alpha Peaks: 600 customers/day generating $18,000/day. Revenue gap of $10,000/day.

questions.prompt: The client proposes reducing Beta Peaks' ticket price to match Alpha Peaks at $30. By what percent should the client expect to increase annual sales?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up an equilibrium equation: customers will switch mountains until wait times equalize. Total customers across both mountains is fixed (no new market entrants). Candidate should also flag the second-order effect: lower price increases volume and raises wait times, which may erode current customers' satisfaction. Strong candidates note the wait time increase from 5 to 20 minutes.

math.setup: Assumptions: customers switch mountains until wait time at each mountain equalizes; no additional customers enter market; all other variables constant (time down mountain, number of lifts, competitor prices); mountain open October through March, 7 days/week, even demand. Let B = number of people in line at Beta Peaks after the price change. Total customers in both lines = 40 (current Beta line) + 360 (current Alpha line) = 400. At equilibrium, wait time at Beta = wait time at Alpha, so: B/8 = (400 - B)/12.
steps: Set up equilibrium: B/8 = (400 - B)/12
Cross multiply: 12B = 8(400 - B) = 3200 - 8B
B = 160 people in line at Beta Peaks after price change

New Beta arrival rate implies new daily customers: 160/5 min wait... actually arrival rate x new wait. Since B=160 and arrival rate = 8/min, new wait = 160/8 = 20 minutes (confirms equilibrium: Alpha line = 400-160=240, wait = 240/12 = 20 min — equal)
New total Beta customers per day: people on lifts (80) + people skiing down (80) + people in line (160) = 320 customers
New daily revenue at Beta: 320 x $30 = $9,600
Old daily revenue at Beta: 200 x $40 = $8,000
Revenue increase per day: $9,600 - $8,000 = $1,600
Percent increase: $1,600 / $8,000 = 20%
math.answer: Beta Peaks should expect a 20% increase in daily (and therefore annual) revenues — from $8,000/day to $9,600/day. However, wait time increases from 5 minutes to 20 minutes, which may negatively impact satisfaction of existing customers.

recommendation: Reduce Beta Peaks day-pass price from $40 to $30 to match Alpha Peaks, which is projected to increase daily revenue by 20% (from $8,000 to $9,600)
Beta Peaks has substantial unused capacity — its 6x shorter wait time signals it can absorb significantly more customers
With equal pricing, customers will redistribute until wait times equalize at 20 minutes, bringing Beta to 320 customers/day vs. the current 200
risks: Wait time will increase from 5 to 20 minutes, which may reduce satisfaction and loyalty among current customers who chose Beta for short queues
The 20% revenue increase assumes no other variables change; if Alpha Peaks responds by further lowering prices, the benefit could erode
Revenue per customer falls from $40 to $30; the volume gain must fully materialize to offset the lower unit price
next_steps: Monitor customer satisfaction and wait times after price reduction
Explore marketing to communicate the shorter lift wait time advantage during the transition
Evaluate whether investing in additional lift capacity could allow Beta Peaks to sustain both higher volume and shorter wait times
Consider seasonal or dynamic pricing strategies to optimize revenue without simply matching competitor pricing
